Central Nervous System
Anatomy
Arterial supply of the brain

This lesson covers how the brain receives its arterial blood: the vertebro-basilar system and the cerebral part of the internal carotid artery, their branches, and the circle of Willis that joins them. It then maps which artery supplies the brainstem, cerebellum and each surface of the cerebrum, and ends with the applied anatomy of motor and sensory deficits after anterior or middle cerebral artery occlusion.

Vertebro-basilar system

The 4th part of the vertebral artery enters the skull through the foramen magnum and unites with its fellow at the lower border of the pons to form the basilar artery. The basilar artery ascends in the midline on the ventral surface of the pons and, at the pons's upper border, ends by dividing into the right and left posterior cerebral arteries.

Branches of the vertebral artery

  • Two posterior spinal arteries.
  • Anterior spinal artery: arises as two arteries, one from each vertebral artery, which then unite.
  • Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA).
  • Meningeal branches: supply the dura mater of the posterior cranial fossa.
  • Medullary arteries: supply the medulla.

Branches of the basilar artery

  • Pontine branches: supply the pons.
  • Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA): supplies the anterior portion of the inferior surface of the cerebellum.
  • Internal auditory (labyrinthine) artery: enters the internal auditory meatus to supply the internal ear.
  • Superior cerebellar artery: supplies the superior surface of the cerebellum.
  • Posterior cerebral artery (PCA): curves around the cerebral peduncle to the medial surface below the splenium of the corpus callosum, then passes in the precalcarine sulcus. It supplies mainly the inferior surface of the cerebrum.

Internal carotid artery (cerebral part)

The internal carotid artery enters the cranial cavity through the carotid canal and takes a sinuous course through the cavernous sinus. It pierces the sinus roof and ends at the anterior perforated substance by dividing into the middle cerebral and anterior cerebral arteries.

Branches

  1. Ophthalmic artery: supplies the orbital structures, including the eyeball.
  2. Posterior communicating artery: runs backwards and anastomoses with the proximal part of the posterior cerebral artery.
  3. Anterior choroidal artery: forms the choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle.
  4. Anterior cerebral artery (ACA): runs forwards above the optic nerve and communicates with its fellow by the anterior communicating artery. It then curves backwards above the corpus callosum on the medial surface, supplying mainly this surface.
  5. Middle cerebral artery (MCA): runs laterally through the stem of the lateral sulcus, then upwards in its posterior ramus to the superolateral surface, supplying mainly this surface.

Artery of cerebral thrombosis: the anterior choroidal artery is the one most susceptible to thrombosis, because of its long subarachnoid course and relatively small lumen.

Circle of Willis (circulus arteriosus)

A circle of anastomosis between branches of the basilar and internal carotid arteries, lying in the interpeduncular fossa.

  • Anteriorly: the anterior communicating and anterior cerebral arteries.
  • Posteriorly: the basilar artery dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries.
  • Laterally, on each side: the posterior communicating artery.

Functional significance: it provides alternative routes for collateral circulation if one of the major arteries forming the circle is blocked.

Arterial supply of the brainstem and cerebellum

RegionArteries
MedullaTwo vertebral arteries; anterior and posterior spinal arteries; anterior and posterior inferior cerebellar arteries; basilar artery
PonsNumerous pontine branches from the basilar artery; anterior inferior cerebellar artery
MidbrainPosterior cerebral artery; superior cerebellar artery; direct branches from the basilar artery; posterior communicating and anterior choroidal arteries
CerebellumSuperior surface: superior cerebellar artery. Inferior surface: anterior part by the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, posterior part by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery

Arterial supply of the cerebrum

SurfaceMain arteryExceptions
SuperolateralMiddle cerebral arteryA narrow strip along the superomedial border up to the parieto-occipital sulcus is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery. A narrow strip along the lower border of the temporal lobe (excluding the temporal pole) and the occipital lobe are supplied by the posterior cerebral artery. The temporal pole is supplied by the middle cerebral artery.
MedialAnterior cerebral arteryThe temporal pole is supplied by the middle cerebral artery; the occipital lobe by the posterior cerebral artery.
InferiorPosterior cerebral arteryThe lateral part of the orbital surface of the frontal lobe and the temporal pole are supplied by the middle cerebral artery; the medial part of the orbital surface of the frontal lobe by the anterior cerebral artery.

Three types of cerebral artery branches

  • Cortical branches: supply the outer portion of the cerebrum.
  • Central branches: supply internal structures, e.g. the corpus callosum and internal capsule.
  • Choroidal branches: project into the ventricles, forming the choroid plexuses.

Applied anatomy

Both the motor area (area 4) and the sensory area (areas 3, 1, 2) are supplied in the same pattern: the upper third by the anterior cerebral artery and the lower two thirds by the middle cerebral artery.

Occluded arteryVoluntary movement affectedSensation affected
Anterior cerebral arteryPerineum and lower limb of the opposite sidePerineum and lower limb of the opposite side
Middle cerebral arteryHead, neck and upper limb of the opposite sideHead, neck and upper limb of the opposite side

Key points / quick review

Vertebro-basilar system

  • Vertebral arteries unite at the lower border of the pons to form the basilar artery, which divides into the two posterior cerebral arteries.
  • Vertebral branches: two posterior spinal, anterior spinal, PICA, meningeal, medullary.
  • Basilar branches: pontine, AICA, internal auditory, superior cerebellar, posterior cerebral.

Internal carotid artery

  • Enters via the carotid canal, passes through the cavernous sinus and ends at the anterior perforated substance as the MCA and ACA.
  • Branches: ophthalmic, posterior communicating, anterior choroidal, ACA, MCA.
  • Anterior choroidal artery is the artery of cerebral thrombosis (long subarachnoid course, small lumen).

Circle of Willis

  • Lies in the interpeduncular fossa.
  • Anterior: anterior communicating and anterior cerebral arteries; posterior: basilar dividing into the PCAs; lateral: posterior communicating arteries.
  • Provides collateral circulation if a major artery is blocked.

Brainstem and cerebellum

  • Pons: pontine branches and AICA.
  • Cerebellum: SCA superiorly; AICA anterior and PICA posterior inferiorly.

Cerebral surfaces

  • Superolateral: MCA. Medial: ACA. Inferior: PCA.
  • The temporal pole is supplied by the MCA.
  • Branch types: cortical, central, choroidal.

Applied anatomy

  • Areas 4 and 3, 1, 2: upper third by ACA, lower two thirds by MCA.
  • ACA occlusion: opposite perineum and lower limb.
  • MCA occlusion: opposite head, neck and upper limb.
